findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of the default JKS KeyStore (i.e. the JDK 'SUN' provider), not a BouncyCastle provider, violating the CryptoProvider contract that this method returns the BC provider. keycloak-common's BouncyIntegration initializes its PROVIDER constant from CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider().getName(); in a standalone authz-client deployment (the exact scenario this provider targets, since AuthzClient.create now triggers detection) that constant resolves to 'SUN', so any later keycloak-common lookup scoped to BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER (e.g. EC KeyFactory for PEM public keys) fails with NoSuchAlgorithmException because SUN does not provide those algorithms. Debugging is hard because the wrong value is baked in at static-init time.

[ADVISORY] detectProvider() silently picks the highest-order provider and demotes all others to a single debug-level log, replacing the previous fail-fast IllegalStateException when multiple CryptoProviders are on the classpath. Environments with a misconfigured classpath (e.g. a FIPS-intended deployment that accidentally still bundles crypto/default, or a server deployment that accidentally packages authz-client's provider) previously crashed at startup with a message naming every provider; now they run with a silently selected provider and the only trace is a debug log nobody enables, so a FIPS-mandated setup can end up running the non-FIPS default provider without any error.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER() contains two dead statements — 'ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);' and 'ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);' — whose results are discarded before the real sequence is built three lines below. Readers and future maintainers must reverse-engineer that these two encoder invocations contribute nothing to the returned bytes; the next change to this conversion (e.g. adding a third encoded component) risks being made against the dead lines instead of the real writeDerSeq call. Deleting the two lines changes no behavior.

[ADVISORY] The test never asserts that the regenerated ASN.1 DER (asn1Des) equals the JDK-produced signature 'sign'; the encoder is only validated against the in-repo decoder, so any encoder producing self-consistent but non-canonical DER passes. concatenatedRSToASN1DER() could emit malformed or non-minimal DER (wrong tag, redundant length octets) and all three ES256/ES384/ES512 tests still pass, because the assertion only checks decoder(encoder(decoder(sign))) == decoder(sign); the actual interoperability requirement — output byte-identical to what the JDK Signature and the Keycloak server produce — is untested, and a regression surfaces only as rejected signatures at runtime against the server.

[ADVISORY] getKeyStore(KeystoreFormat) resolves the format via KeyStore.getInstance(format.name()) against the default JVM providers, so the BCFKS enum value throws KeyStoreException ('BCFKS not found') because no BC provider is registered by this provider. An operator or out-of-tree caller that routes KeystoreUtil keystore loading through this CryptoProvider with KeystoreFormat.BCFKS gets a KeyStoreException at runtime even though the format is a supported KeystoreUtil enum value in keycloak-common; nothing in this diff calls it, so it is latent rather than immediately reachable.

[BUG] detectProvider silently selects the highest-order provider instead of failing when multiple CryptoProviders are on the classpath, and DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so ties are resolved by nondeterministic ServiceLoader discovery order. A FIPS deployment that accidentally ships both keycloak-crypto-fips1402 and keycloak-crypto-default on the classpath previously failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded'; it now silently starts using whichever of the two order-200 providers ServiceLoader happens to load first, so a misconfigured FIPS install runs non-FIPS crypto with no error. The tie between the three order-200 providers has no defined winner.

[ADVISORY] The test only asserts the round-trip rsConcat == rsConcat2 and never asserts that asn1Des equals the original JDK-produced DER signature `sign`, so the two conversion functions are only verified to be inverses of each other, not to be correct. Any symmetric defect in concatenatedRSToASN1DER that produces valid-to-itself but non-canonical or malformed DER (e.g. non-minimal lengths or non-minimal INTEGER encoding) passes all three test methods, because the test's own decoder accepts the same non-canonical output; the first signal is a third-party JWT/verifier implementation rejecting signatures the authz client emits, which is exactly the interoperability scenario this provider exists for.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER contains two dead statements (`ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);`) whose encoders are created, written to, and then discarded without ever being read. The next reader of this crypto code must reverse-engineer that these two lines have no effect (and suspect a half-finished refactor that dropped the encoders on the floor), and any copy of this block into real usage reproduces the confusion; the lines allocate two ByteArrayOutputStreams per signature for nothing.

[ADVISORY] readNext() misparses indefinite-length elements: readLength() returns -1 for 0x80, then `length += reset()` turns it into the header byte count, and read(length) consumes the length octet itself as element content instead of throwing. A DER structure containing an indefinite-length element (legal in BER, rejected by DER) is silently decoded into garbage bytes rather than failing with the IOException every other malformed-input path in this decoder produces, so a corrupted signature yields a silently wrong concatenated RS value instead of a clean parse error.

[ADVISORY] readSequence() never validates that the declared SEQUENCE length matches the bytes actually consumed: the loop decrements `length` by each element's size and exits on any negative value, so elements totalling more than the declared length are accepted and trailing bytes are silently ignored. asn1derToConcatenatedRS accepts structurally invalid signatures (e.g. a SEQUENCE declaring length 8 containing two 6-byte elements plus 4 trailing garbage bytes) and returns values parsed from them, deferring failure to a confusing downstream signature-verification error instead of a DER format error at the parse site.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten multi-provider detection (order-based sorting, silent ignore of lower-order providers, removal of the size>1 exception) has no test coverage anywhere in this diff — the only test added is ECDSAAlgorithmTest, which never touches detectProvider. A regression in the ordering or tie-breaking (e.g. an accidental comparator sign flip) silently changes which crypto provider every Keycloak deployment selects, with no test failure to catch it; this is a non-trivial behavior change to a load-bearing selection path shipped with zero verification.

[ADVISORY] order() is added to the public CryptoProvider SPI as a required abstract method with no default implementation, breaking compile and binary compatibility for every out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation. Any external or downstream implementation of CryptoProvider (the interface exists precisely so alternate crypto stacks can plug in) stops compiling and fails at linkage on upgrade; a default method returning 0 would have preserved compatibility while giving the three in-tree providers their explicit orders.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of the default JVM KeyStore type (e.g. SUN on HotSpot), not BouncyCastle, despite the method's contract and name. Any code path that calls CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting a BC provider (the pattern used throughout keycloak services for provider-scoped crypto lookups) silently receives SUN/SunRsaSign and gets different algorithm behavior or a NoSuchProviderException, with no error pointing at this implementation.

[ADVISORY] The ServiceLoader registration makes AuthzClientCryptoProvider globally selectable on any classpath containing authz-client, yet 12 of its 15 CryptoProvider methods throw UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet."). An application that adds authz-client as a dependency and calls CryptoIntegration.init with no higher-order provider present gets this partial provider selected; any other component on the same classpath then crashes at runtime with UnsupportedOperationException from getPemUtils()/getSignature()/etc., where before this change the same classpath failed at init with the clear 'Not able to load any cryptoProvider' message.

[BUG] detectProvider() silently selects the highest-order provider when multiple CryptoProviders are on the classpath instead of failing fast, a global behavior change to the shared common module made solely to accommodate the new authz-client provider. Every existing consumer of keycloak-common (server, adapters) loses the loud 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' IllegalStateException that caught classpath misconfigurations; a deployment with e.g. both crypto-default and crypto-fips1402 (both order() == 200) now silently picks whichever ServiceLoader returns first, so the wrong crypto stack can be in effect with only a debug-level log ('Ignored crypto providers: ...') as a trace. This side effect is not traceable to the stated intent of adding an authz-client provider and should be gated or at least logged at warn.

[ADVISORY] Adding the abstract method order() to the public CryptoProvider SPI interface breaks source and binary compatibility for every out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation. Third-party code implementing org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider (a documented extension point used for custom FIPS/BC integrations) fails to compile against the new interface and throws AbstractMethodError at runtime when an old compiled provider is loaded, because the diff only patches the three in-tree implementations (default, elytron, fips1402). A default method returning a low order would have avoided this public-surface break.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER contains two dead statements — ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger) and ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger) — whose results are created and immediately discarded before the real encoding happens via a third encoder. The lines execute on every ECDSA signature conversion and produce output that is never used, a copy-paste leftover that misleads readers into thinking the individual encoders matter; the next person touching this method has to reverse-engineer whether the discarded encoders are intentional before they can safely change the actual return path.

[ADVISORY] Registering the partial AuthzClientCryptoProvider (order 100) via ServiceLoader makes it the sole detected provider in any JVM whose classpath has keycloak-common + authz-client but no other provider, replacing the previous clear detection error with UnsupportedOperationException for every unimplemented CryptoProvider method. Code sharing that classpath that uses keycloak-common facilities other than ECDSA R/S conversion (e.g. PemUtils routing through CryptoIntegration.getPemUtils(), getSignature(), getAlgorithmProvider()) previously failed with IllegalStateException 'Not able to load any cryptoProvider' and now crashes with UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.') from an unrelated authz-client jar; 17 of the 19 interface methods on this provider are unimplemented throwers, so the provider overstates what it can serve.

[ADVISORY] The test instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly, so none of the new selection logic this diff introduces — the META-INF/services registration, the order()-based sorting in detectProvider, or the CryptoIntegration.init call added to AuthzClient.create(Configuration) — is exercised by any test. A regression in the ServiceLoader registration (wrong class name, missing resource) or in the ordering change in CryptoIntegration would pass the whole test suite while the feature is broken at runtime; the ordering semantics in particular is the riskiest new behavior in the diff and is the piece with zero coverage.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of KeyStore.getDefaultType() (SunJSSE for the default 'pkcs12'/'jks' keystores), not a BouncyCastle provider, contradicting the method's contract as implemented by every other CryptoProvider. Any caller that uses getBouncyCastleProvider() to locate or register the BC provider (the reason the method exists in default/fips/elytron providers) silently receives SunJSSE instead; today nothing in this diff calls it, but the provider is public API and the mismatch surfaces only when a consumer of the shared interface invokes it against this implementation.

[BUG] detectProvider now silently selects the highest-order provider when multiple CryptoProviders are on the classpath, and when two providers share the same order value (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return 200) the stable sort leaves the pick to ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order. A misconfigured classpath that previously failed fast with 'Make sure only one cryptoProvider available on the classpath' now boots silently with an arbitrary provider: a FIPS deployment that accidentally ships both crypto/default and crypto/fips1402 jars runs non-FIPS crypto with no error, and which provider wins can differ between environments because the tie is resolved by classpath order, not by any deterministic rule.

[ADVISORY] ASN1Encoder and ASN1Decoder (~300 new lines) re-implement the ECDSA concatenated-RS <-> ASN.1-DER conversion that already exists in keycloak-core's org.keycloak.crypto.ECDSAAlgorithm (the very class the new test imports for the ECDSAAlgorithm enum), creating a second parallel implementation of the same domain logic. Two independent DER conversion implementations now exist in the codebase; a fix to one (e.g., handling of a malformed length or leading-zero edge case) will not propagate to the other, and future maintainers signing/verifying via different paths get subtly different behavior. If the duplication exists to avoid the BouncyCastle dependency keycloak-core's version drags in, nothing in the code or javadoc records that rationale, so the next reviewer cannot distinguish accidental duplication from deliberate decoupling.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER contains two dead statements — ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger) and ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger) — whose results are discarded before the real return expression re-encodes both integers into a fresh encoder. Two throwaway encoders are allocated and populated on every ECDSA signature conversion (a per-token hot path), and the orphaned lines read like part of the encoding so the next editor 'fixing' the method risks wiring the discarded encoders into the return and corrupting the signature format; the actual output comes only from the third encoder.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of a default-type KeyStore (KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()), which on a standard JVM is 'SUN'/JDK, not BouncyCastle, violating the method's contract as the accessor for the BouncyCastle provider. Any caller (present or future, including shared keycloak-common utilities that resolve BC-specific algorithms through CryptoIntegration.getBouncyCastleProvider()) that uses the returned provider for a BC-only algorithm gets NoSuchAlgorithmException or ProviderMismatchException at runtime, and the failure points at the algorithm lookup rather than at this silently-wrong provider binding; it also constructs and discards a KeyStore instance on every call.

[ADVISORY] order() is added to the public CryptoProvider SPI as an abstract method with no default implementation, so every out-of-tree implementer of this interface fails to compile against the new version. Third-party and downstream custom CryptoProvider implementations (the interface is a public extension point in org.keycloak.common.crypto) break on upgrade; a default method returning e.g. 0 would have kept them source-compatible while still letting the three in-tree providers declare explicit precedence.

[ADVISORY] The test instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly, so none of the production wiring added in this diff is exercised: the new META-INF/services registration, the CryptoIntegration.init call in AuthzClient.create, and the new order-based selection logic in detectProvider all run only in production. A regression in exactly the machinery this PR exists to add — a mistyped service-file class name, a wrong order() value relative to the server providers, or the init call landing on the wrong AuthzClient.create overload — keeps the test suite green while every standalone AuthzClient deployment fails at first use with 'Not able to load any cryptoProvider' or silently picks the wrong provider.

[BUG] The detectProvider change silently replaces the previous hard-fail contract ('Multiple crypto providers loaded... Make sure only one cryptoProvider available on the classpath') with silent highest-order selection logged only at debug level, changing the objective from 'fail loudly on ambiguous classpath' to 'silently tolerate misconfiguration' without any warn/error-level signal. Deployments that previously aborted at startup on a duplicate-provider classpath (e.g., a FIPS-aware deployment where an extra provider jar is accidentally present, or an embedder who relied on the error to catch classpath pollution) now boot successfully with an arbitrarily selected provider; the 'Ignored crypto providers' list is written only via logger.debugf, so operators get no warning at default log levels, and a wrong-provider selection surfaces later as runtime failures (e.g., UnsupportedOperationException from AuthzClientCryptoProvider methods) far from the actual misconfiguration.

[ADVISORY] Adding the abstract order() method to the public CryptoProvider interface breaks compilation of every out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation (custom embedders, downstream forks) that existed before this change, since the method has no default implementation. Any external implementor upgrading to this version gets a compile error on their custom provider; the interface constraint changed as a side effect of a PR whose stated intent is only to add an authz-client provider, with no deprecation cycle or default method to preserve source compatibility.

[ADVISORY] AuthzClient.create now unconditionally initializes CryptoIntegration, so applications that previously failed fast at create() with IllegalStateException ('Not able to load any cryptoProvider') now instead succeed and obtain AuthzClientCryptoProvider, whose getPemUtils(), getAlgorithmProvider(), getSignature(), etc. throw UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.') at point of use. Client applications that call other CryptoIntegration-backed functionality (e.g., PEM parsing of certificates/keys, JWT algorithm providers) get a deferred UnsupportedOperationException with placeholder message text at runtime instead of the deterministic startup error they got before; the failure mode moved from init-time to first-use-time and the message gives no hint about which capability is missing.

[ADVISORY] The statements 'ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);' and 'ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);' are dead code — their results are discarded and the return statement below re-encodes both values from scratch. Readers of the signature-conversion code cannot tell whether these writes are semantically required (they look like stateful encoding steps but are not), and the leftover lines signal an incomplete refactor from an earlier iteration; the next person changing this method risks 'fixing' the apparent duplicate encoding incorrectly.

[BUG] readInteger() passes the indefinite-length sentinel returned by readLength() (-1 for 0x80) straight into read(-1), which executes new byte[-1] and throws an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException instead of the declared IOException. asn1derToConcatenatedRS() parses attacker-controlled DER signature bytes from submitted JWTs (ES256/384/512); a token whose signature contains an INTEGER with length 0x80 makes the verification path throw NegativeArraySizeException, an unchecked exception that escapes the method's IOException contract and bypasses whatever invalid-signature error handling the caller has (e.g., surfacing as an unhandled 500 instead of a token-rejection path).

[ADVISORY] detectProvider() replaces the previous fail-fast IllegalStateException for multiple crypto providers with silent resolution by order(), logging the ignored providers only at debug level. Operators lose the hard signal that the classpath has ambiguous crypto providers: a misconfigured or contaminated deployment (e.g., a FIPS environment where a non-FIPS provider with a higher order() value is present) now silently runs with whichever provider sorted first, and the conflict is invisible at default log levels. The old code was fail-closed; the new code is fail-open with a debug-only audit trail.

[ADVISORY] AuthzClient.create() now triggers CryptoIntegration.init() with the authz-client's own classloader, mutating process-global crypto provider state as a side effect of client construction. In a shared JVM (an app embedding authz-client alongside other Keycloak components/adapters), the first AuthzClient.create() call can lock the global CryptoProvider to AuthzClientCryptoProvider when that is the only provider its classloader can see; every later crypto operation routed through CryptoIntegration.getProvider() that touches the unsupported methods (getSignature, getAlgorithmProvider, getPemUtils, getAesCbcCipher — all 'throw new UnsupportedOperationException') fails, turning previously working token/crypto code in unrelated components into runtime failures.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of the default KeyStore (typically the JDK 'SUN' provider), not a BouncyCastle provider, despite the interface contract and its name. Callers that use this provider for BC-specific capabilities (PEM/EC parsing, BC-only algorithms) silently get the JDK provider instead: BC-only operations fail at runtime, and in a FIPS-constrained standalone authz-client deployment the non-validated default JDK provider is what gets registered as the crypto provider rather than a FIPS-validated one — a silent crypto-downgrade path with no error at selection time.

[ADVISORY] The only tests for the new ASN.1 codec are encode/decode round-trips on well-formed signatures generated by the JDK; there is no test feeding malformed or adversarial DER (truncated buffers, indefinite lengths, non-INTEGER elements, over-long lengths) into asn1derToConcatenatedRS. asn1derToConcatenatedRS is a parser of untrusted input (JWT signature bytes chosen by the token sender), and its error behavior on malformed input (including the NegativeArraySizeException path in ASN1Decoder.readInteger) is untested; any regression that turns a parsing failure into an unchecked exception or a lenient accept will ship unnoticed because the suite only exercises the happy path.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER() builds two ASN1Encoder instances and writes r and s into them, then discards both and re-encodes from scratch in the actual return statement — dead work executed on every ECDSA sign/verify conversion. Every signature conversion performs two wasted encodings, and the dead statements mislead maintainers into thinking they contribute to the result (e.g., someone 'fixing' ordering or padding will edit the discarded encoders and see no effect); deleting the two ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) lines removes the confusion with zero behavior change.

[BUG] The test only asserts a self-consistent round trip (rsConcat -> asn1Des -> rsConcat2 equals rsConcat) and never compares the re-encoded DER signature (asn1Des) against the original real Java-produced DER signature (sign), so the encoder direction is verified only against the decoder in the same class. If concatenatedRSToASN1DER emits a non-conformant DER encoding (e.g. non-minimal length octets or a wrong tag from ASN1Encoder.writeDerSeq/writeLength), asn1derToConcatenatedRS reads it back symmetrically and Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2) still passes, while every external JWT/JOSE verifier that receives the DER signature rejects it — the suite reports green on broken crypto output. Asserting Assert.assertArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des) at line 57 would close this.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten detectProvider logic (order-based sorting, silent demotion of lower-order providers instead of the previous IllegalStateException on multiple providers) has no test coverage anywhere in this diff; the only test file added is authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java, which never references CryptoIntegration (checked: it is the sole spec/test file in the diff). A regression in the new selection logic — e.g. the reversed() comparator accidentally dropped so the authz client's order-100 AuthzClientCryptoProvider loses to a co-classpath'd default provider, or the sort is inverted — silently selects the wrong CryptoProvider with no failing test; downstream users get UnsupportedOperationException from the wrong provider's getAlgorithmProvider/getSignature at runtime with no CI signal.

[ADVISORY] The new test exercises only the happy path: none of the error branches added in this diff are ever triggered — the seq.size() != 2 guard in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS, and the EOFException/IOException paths in ASN1Decoder.readTag/readTagNumber/readLength/read (checked: ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java is the only test file in the diff and it feeds only well-formed Java-generated signatures through the decoder). Malformed or truncated DER signature input reaches production completely unexercised; a regression that turns a validation IOException into e.g. an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException or an unbounded read on attacker-controlled signature bytes would pass CI, and the guard messages promised by the code ('Invalid sequence with size different to 2', 'corrupted stream - out of bounds length found') are never verified to actually fire.

[ADVISORY] The statements 'ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);' and 'ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);' construct two encoders whose results are discarded; the return value is built independently three lines later, and the round-trip test passes with these lines present or removed, so nothing in the suite detects that they are dead. Every ES256/384/512 signature conversion allocates two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances, and more importantly the dead lines mislead maintainers into believing the individual INTEGER encodings are intentionally pre-built (e.g. for reuse or side effects); a future edit that 'fixes' the sequence to use these pre-built encoders would silently change behavior with no test distinguishing intent, because the existing tests are insensitive to both states.

[BUG] readInteger() passes readLength()'s -1 indefinite-length sentinel directly into read(length), so `new byte[length]` with length=-1 throws NegativeArraySizeException instead of the IOException the method contract declares. A DER signature containing an indefinite-length INTEGER element (0x80 length octet) makes asn1derToConcatenatedRS blow up with a raw NegativeArraySizeException — an untyped RuntimeException the IOException-based error path cannot catch or translate, so malformed/corrupt signature input surfaces as an unhandled 500-class failure at whatever call site invokes signature conversion instead of a handled parse failure.

[ADVISORY] detectProvider() replaces the hard failure on multiple loaded CryptoProviders with silent highest-order() selection and logs the ignored providers only at debug level. An operator with a classpath misconfiguration (e.g., DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider both present, both order()=200) that previously failed fast at startup with an actionable message now silently runs with whichever provider ServiceLoader enumerates first — nondeterministic with respect to classpath ordering — and the only trace is a debug-level 'Ignored crypto providers' line nobody sees in production, so FIPS-compliance misconfigurations go unnoticed until an audit.

[ADVISORY] Most CryptoProvider methods (getAlgorithmProvider, getPemUtils, getCertificateUtils, getSignature, getAesCbcCipher, getAesGcmCipher, etc.) are unimplemented stubs throwing UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.'), deferring the failure from init to first use. With only the authz-client artifact on the classpath, CryptoIntegration.init() now succeeds (order 100 provider found), so any code path that routes through CryptoIntegration for a non-ECDSA operation — e.g., PEM key parsing or AES-based token decryption shared-code — previously failed at startup with 'Not able to load any cryptoProvider' but now reaches runtime and dies with an UnsupportedOperationException, moving the failure from an early, clear signal to a mid-operation crash far from the configuration cause.

[BUG] readSequence() silently returns an empty list for an indefinite-length (0x80) sequence because readLength() returns -1 and the `while (length > 0)` loop never executes, never consuming or validating any content. Corrupt DER input with indefinite-length encoding is reported to the caller as 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2' from asn1derToConcatenatedRS, a misleading error that misdirects debugging toward a sequence-size problem when the actual defect is an unsupported length encoding; readNext() on such an element similarly computes a garbage length (-1 + header bytes consumed) and re-reads from the mark, producing a nonsense element.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()), which on a stock JDK resolves to SUN for PKCS12, not BouncyCastle. Any caller that uses this provider handle to look up or register BC-specific algorithms gets SUN back and fails with NoSuchAlgorithmException (or silently takes a non-BC code path); the name promises BC but the implementation returns whatever provider owns the default keystore type, and a fresh KeyStore instance is constructed per call purely to extract that provider.

[ADVISORY] integerToBytes() silently truncates the high-order bytes when qLength < bytes.length, so an r or s value larger than the curve length is chopped instead of rejected. A malformed DER signature whose r/s exceed the component length yields a silently corrupted concatenated signature that fails verification (or signature generation) far downstream with no indication the DER was invalid, sending debuggers hunting through the verification layer instead of pointing at the malformed input; the correct behavior is an IOException, as the seq.size()!=2 check already does for other malformations.

[ADVISORY] The two standalone statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` build encoders whose output is discarded — dead code with no effect on the result. A maintainer reading concatenatedRSToASN1DER can reasonably conclude these encoders contribute to the returned DER (they appear to pre-encode r/s before the real return statement), and any future change to the r/s encoding applied to only one of the three duplicated write sites produces an encoder that passes the round-trip test while diverging in production; both lines pass the deletion test — removing them changes nothing.

adjudication.rationale: The new test `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` directly does `new AuthzClientCryptoProvider()` and calls `prov.getEcdsaCryptoProvider()` instead of exercising the production integration path added in this diff: the SPI registration file `authz/client/src/main/resources/META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider`, the new `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` call in `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)`, and the new order-based provider selection in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` (`ServiceLoader...sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())`). As a result, regressions in those wiring pieces (service file classname, order values, or calling the wrong `AuthzClient.create` overload) would not be caught by the test suite even though they could break standalone AuthzClient usage.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The detectProvider change silently replaces the previous hard-fail contract ('Multiple crypto providers loaded... Make sure only one cryptoProvider available on the classpath') with silent highest-order selection logged only at debug level, changing the objective from 'fail loudly on ambiguous classpath' to 'silently tolerate misconfiguration' without any warn/error-level signal. Deployments that previously aborted at startup on a duplicate-provider classpath (e.g., a FIPS-aware deployment where an extra provider jar is accidentally present, or an embedder who relied on the error to catch classpath pollution) now boot successfully with an arbitrarily selected provider; the 'Ignored crypto providers' list is written only via logger.debugf, so operators get no warning at default log levels, and a wrong-provider selection surfaces later as runtime failures (e.g., UnsupportedOperationException from AuthzClientCryptoProvider methods) far from the actual misconfiguration.

adjudication.rationale: The diff verifiably changes `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(...)` from throwing on `foundProviders.size() > 1` to selecting the highest-`order()` provider (`.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())`) and only emitting a `logger.debugf` message listing ignored providers. This is an intentional behavioral shift enabled by the new `CryptoProvider#order()` API, not an intrinsic correctness defect, but it does create an operational/diagnostic concern: ambiguous/misconfigured classpaths that previously failed fast will now proceed without any warn/error-level signal.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Adding the abstract order() method to the public CryptoProvider interface breaks compilation of every out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation (custom embedders, downstream forks) that existed before this change, since the method has no default implementation. Any external implementor upgrading to this version gets a compile error on their custom provider; the interface constraint changed as a side effect of a PR whose stated intent is only to add an authz-client provider, with no deprecation cycle or default method to preserve source compatibility.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new abstract method `int order();` to the public `org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` interface (common/src/main/java/.../CryptoProvider.java) with no default implementation. While in-repo implementations were updated (e.g., DefaultCryptoProvider/WildFlyElytronProvider/FIPS1402Provider/AuthzClientCryptoProvider now implement `order()`), any external/out-of-tree implementation compiled against this updated interface would fail to compile until it adds the method. That’s a real, diff-grounded source-compatibility/API break, not a runtime correctness defect within this PR’s code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] AuthzClient.create now unconditionally initializes CryptoIntegration, so applications that previously failed fast at create() with IllegalStateException ('Not able to load any cryptoProvider') now instead succeed and obtain AuthzClientCryptoProvider, whose getPemUtils(), getAlgorithmProvider(), getSignature(), etc. throw UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.') at point of use. Client applications that call other CryptoIntegration-backed functionality (e.g., PEM parsing of certificates/keys, JWT algorithm providers) get a deferred UnsupportedOperationException with placeholder message text at runtime instead of the deterministic startup error they got before; the failure mode moved from init-time to first-use-time and the message gives no hint about which capability is missing.

adjudication.rationale: The diff makes `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` unconditionally call `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`, and the authz-client module now contributes a `CryptoProvider` via `META-INF/services/...` (`AuthzClientCryptoProvider`). That provider implements `order()` but most required `CryptoProvider` methods (`getPemUtils()`, `getAlgorithmProvider()`, `getSignature()`, etc.) throw `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.")`. Therefore, in an environment where no other crypto provider is present on the classpath, initialization will now succeed (provider is found) but later usage of many CryptoIntegration-backed capabilities will fail at runtime with a deferred, non-informative `UnsupportedOperationException`, instead of failing deterministically at init-time when no provider existed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The statements 'ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);' and 'ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);' are dead code — their results are discarded and the return statement below re-encodes both values from scratch. Readers of the signature-conversion code cannot tell whether these writes are semantically required (they look like stateful encoding steps but are not), and the leftover lines signal an incomplete refactor from an earlier iteration; the next person changing this method risks 'fixing' the apparent duplicate encoding incorrectly.

adjudication.rationale: In `AuthzClientCryptoProvider#getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER(...)`, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` each create a new `ASN1Encoder`, write into it, and then discard it without using `toByteArray()` or passing it onward. The subsequent `return` re-creates new encoders and re-encodes both integers again inside `writeDerSeq(...)`, so those two earlier writes are redundant/dead and can mislead readers into thinking they are required stateful steps.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] readInteger() passes the indefinite-length sentinel returned by readLength() (-1 for 0x80) straight into read(-1), which executes new byte[-1] and throws an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException instead of the declared IOException. asn1derToConcatenatedRS() parses attacker-controlled DER signature bytes from submitted JWTs (ES256/384/512); a token whose signature contains an INTEGER with length 0x80 makes the verification path throw NegativeArraySizeException, an unchecked exception that escapes the method's IOException contract and bypasses whatever invalid-signature error handling the caller has (e.g., surfacing as an unhandled 500 instead of a token-rejection path).

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `ASN1Decoder.readInteger()`, `int length = readLength();` can return `-1` when the length byte is `0x80` (indefinite-length), per `readLength()` implementation. That `-1` is then passed directly to `read(length)`, which does `new byte[length]` and will throw an unchecked `NegativeArraySizeException` rather than the declared `IOException`. This is verifiable from the diff. `asn1derToConcatenatedRS()` calls `ASN1Decoder.create(seq.get(0)).readInteger()` / `readInteger()` on provided DER signature bytes, so malformed input can trigger this path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] detectProvider() replaces the previous fail-fast IllegalStateException for multiple crypto providers with silent resolution by order(), logging the ignored providers only at debug level. Operators lose the hard signal that the classpath has ambiguous crypto providers: a misconfigured or contaminated deployment (e.g., a FIPS environment where a non-FIPS provider with a higher order() value is present) now silently runs with whichever provider sorted first, and the conflict is invisible at default log levels. The old code was fail-closed; the new code is fail-open with a debug-only audit trail.

adjudication.rationale: The diff in CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() removes the previous IllegalStateException when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are found and instead sorts providers by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and returns the first, only logging the rest at debug level. This matches the finding: ambiguity on the classpath is no longer fail-fast/visible by default, and selection becomes implicit based on order(). While this is a significant operational/security posture change, the diff shows it as intentional behavior (new order() API and implementations), so it’s better classified as a design/operability concern rather than a verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] AuthzClient.create() now triggers CryptoIntegration.init() with the authz-client's own classloader, mutating process-global crypto provider state as a side effect of client construction. In a shared JVM (an app embedding authz-client alongside other Keycloak components/adapters), the first AuthzClient.create() call can lock the global CryptoProvider to AuthzClientCryptoProvider when that is the only provider its classloader can see; every later crypto operation routed through CryptoIntegration.getProvider() that touches the unsupported methods (getSignature, getAlgorithmProvider, getPemUtils, getAesCbcCipher — all 'throw new UnsupportedOperationException') fails, turning previously working token/crypto code in unrelated components into runtime failures.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` now calls `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`, which (per `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider`) uses `ServiceLoader.load(CryptoProvider, classLoader)` and selects a single provider that is cached process-wide. This PR also adds a `META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` entry in the authz-client module pointing to `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, and that provider implements many `CryptoProvider` methods by `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.")` (e.g., `getSignature`, `getAlgorithmProvider`, `getPemUtils`, `getAesCbcCipher`, etc.). Therefore, if `AuthzClient`’s classloader only sees this provider (or it ends up being selected), the global `CryptoIntegration` provider becomes one that can crash unrelated crypto operations at runtime—this is a concrete, diff-grounded behavioral regression caused by client construction mutating global crypto state.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of the default KeyStore (typically the JDK 'SUN' provider), not a BouncyCastle provider, despite the interface contract and its name. Callers that use this provider for BC-specific capabilities (PEM/EC parsing, BC-only algorithms) silently get the JDK provider instead: BC-only operations fail at runtime, and in a FIPS-constrained standalone authz-client deployment the non-validated default JDK provider is what gets registered as the crypto provider rather than a FIPS-validated one — a silent crypto-downgrade path with no error at selection time.

adjudication.rationale: In the new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (registered via `META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider`), `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which returns the provider for the default JDK keystore type (typically a JDK provider like `SUN`/`SUNJSSE`), not a BouncyCastle provider. This contradicts the `CryptoProvider` method name/contract (“Get the bouncycastle provider”) and differs from other implementations in the diff (e.g., `DefaultCryptoProvider`/`FIPS1402Provider` returning actual BC providers). Since `AuthzClient.create()` now calls `CryptoIntegration.init(...)`, this provider can be auto-selected and expose the wrong provider to callers, leading to runtime failures or unintended provider selection.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The only tests for the new ASN.1 codec are encode/decode round-trips on well-formed signatures generated by the JDK; there is no test feeding malformed or adversarial DER (truncated buffers, indefinite lengths, non-INTEGER elements, over-long lengths) into asn1derToConcatenatedRS. asn1derToConcatenatedRS is a parser of untrusted input (JWT signature bytes chosen by the token sender), and its error behavior on malformed input (including the NegativeArraySizeException path in ASN1Decoder.readInteger) is untested; any regression that turns a parsing failure into an unchecked exception or a lenient accept will ship unnoticed because the suite only exercises the happy path.

adjudication.rationale: The new ASN.1 parser can throw unchecked exceptions on malformed/untrusted input. In `ASN1Decoder.readLength()`, a length byte of `0x80` returns `-1` (indefinite length). `ASN1Decoder.readInteger()` and `readNext()` do not guard against `-1` and call `read(length)`, which allocates `new byte[length]`; with `length == -1` this results in a `NegativeArraySizeException` (unchecked) rather than an `IOException`. Since `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` feeds attacker-controlled signature bytes into `ASN1Decoder.create(...).readSequence()`/`readInteger()`, this is a real robustness/security defect exposed by the diff; the test added (`ECDSAAlgorithmTest`) only exercises well-formed signatures and would not catch this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER() builds two ASN1Encoder instances and writes r and s into them, then discards both and re-encodes from scratch in the actual return statement — dead work executed on every ECDSA sign/verify conversion. Every signature conversion performs two wasted encodings, and the dead statements mislead maintainers into thinking they contribute to the result (e.g., someone 'fixing' ordering or padding will edit the discarded encoders and see no effect); deleting the two ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) lines removes the confusion with zero behavior change.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER(), the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` each create an encoder, write a value, and then discard the instance without using its output. The returned value is built by a separate `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger), ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger))...`. This is verifiable dead work on every call and can mislead maintainers, but it does not change correctness of the returned encoding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The test only asserts a self-consistent round trip (rsConcat -> asn1Des -> rsConcat2 equals rsConcat) and never compares the re-encoded DER signature (asn1Des) against the original real Java-produced DER signature (sign), so the encoder direction is verified only against the decoder in the same class. If concatenatedRSToASN1DER emits a non-conformant DER encoding (e.g. non-minimal length octets or a wrong tag from ASN1Encoder.writeDerSeq/writeLength), asn1derToConcatenatedRS reads it back symmetrically and Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2) still passes, while every external JWT/JOSE verifier that receives the DER signature rejects it — the suite reports green on broken crypto output. Asserting Assert.assertArrayEquals(sign, asn1Des) at line 57 would close this.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added ECDSAAlgorithmTest, the test flow is: `sign` (Java DER) -> decode to `rsConcat` -> re-encode to `asn1Des` -> decode to `rsConcat2`, and it only asserts `rsConcat == rsConcat2`. There is no assertion that `asn1Des` matches the original Java-produced DER `sign`, so the encoder is only validated against the paired decoder in AuthzClientCryptoProvider/ASN1Encoder/ASN1Decoder, not against an external/known-good DER encoding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The rewritten detectProvider logic (order-based sorting, silent demotion of lower-order providers instead of the previous IllegalStateException on multiple providers) has no test coverage anywhere in this diff; the only test file added is authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java, which never references CryptoIntegration (checked: it is the sole spec/test file in the diff). A regression in the new selection logic — e.g. the reversed() comparator accidentally dropped so the authz client's order-100 AuthzClientCryptoProvider loses to a co-classpath'd default provider, or the sort is inverted — silently selects the wrong CryptoProvider with no failing test; downstream users get UnsupportedOperationException from the wrong provider's getAlgorithmProvider/getSignature at runtime with no CI signal.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() from throwing on multiple CryptoProvider implementations to sorting them by the new CryptoProvider::order() (descending) and silently choosing the first while only debug-logging the rest (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java). The only added test (authz/client/src/test/java/.../ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java) exercises ASN.1/ECDSA conversion via AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly and never calls CryptoIntegration or validates provider-selection behavior. No other tests in the diff cover the new ordering/selection semantics, so a regression in the comparator/order handling would not be caught by CI.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new test exercises only the happy path: none of the error branches added in this diff are ever triggered — the seq.size() != 2 guard in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS, and the EOFException/IOException paths in ASN1Decoder.readTag/readTagNumber/readLength/read (checked: ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java is the only test file in the diff and it feeds only well-formed Java-generated signatures through the decoder). Malformed or truncated DER signature input reaches production completely unexercised; a regression that turns a validation IOException into e.g. an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException or an unbounded read on attacker-controlled signature bytes would pass CI, and the guard messages promised by the code ('Invalid sequence with size different to 2', 'corrupted stream - out of bounds length found') are never verified to actually fire.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds nontrivial DER parsing/validation logic with multiple error/guard branches (e.g., AuthzClientCryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS checks seq.size()!=2 and ASN1Decoder throws EOFException/IOException in readTag/readTagNumber/readLength/read). The only added test (ECDSAAlgorithmTest) feeds signatures produced by Java Signature.sign(), which are well-formed DER, so none of these newly added error paths are exercised or asserted. This is a specific, diff-grounded test gap around newly introduced validation behavior, not a demonstrable functional defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The statements 'ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);' and 'ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);' construct two encoders whose results are discarded; the return value is built independently three lines later, and the round-trip test passes with these lines present or removed, so nothing in the suite detects that they are dead. Every ES256/384/512 signature conversion allocates two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances, and more importantly the dead lines mislead maintainers into believing the individual INTEGER encodings are intentionally pre-built (e.g. for reuse or side effects); a future edit that 'fixes' the sequence to use these pre-built encoders would silently change behavior with no test distinguishing intent, because the existing tests are insensitive to both states.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` each allocate an ASN1Encoder and write to it, but the resulting encoders/bytes are never used. The method then independently constructs the returned DER sequence using new encoders inside `writeDerSeq(...)`. This is diff-verifiable dead work (extra allocations) and potentially misleading to maintainers, but it does not change correctness because the actual returned value is built from the later `writeDerSeq(...)` call.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] readInteger() passes readLength()'s -1 indefinite-length sentinel directly into read(length), so `new byte[length]` with length=-1 throws NegativeArraySizeException instead of the IOException the method contract declares. A DER signature containing an indefinite-length INTEGER element (0x80 length octet) makes asn1derToConcatenatedRS blow up with a raw NegativeArraySizeException — an untyped RuntimeException the IOException-based error path cannot catch or translate, so malformed/corrupt signature input surfaces as an unhandled 500-class failure at whatever call site invokes signature conversion instead of a handled parse failure.

adjudication.rationale: In `ASN1Decoder.readInteger()`, `int length = readLength();` can return `-1` for the 0x80 indefinite-length form (`readLength()` explicitly returns `-1`). That value is then passed directly to `read(length)`, which does `new byte[length]` without validating `length >= 0`, causing `NegativeArraySizeException` (an unchecked runtime exception) instead of an `IOException`. This can surface via `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.ECDSACryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS()` when parsing malformed DER/ASN.1 signatures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] detectProvider() replaces the hard failure on multiple loaded CryptoProviders with silent highest-order() selection and logs the ignored providers only at debug level. An operator with a classpath misconfiguration (e.g., DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider both present, both order()=200) that previously failed fast at startup with an actionable message now silently runs with whichever provider ServiceLoader enumerates first — nondeterministic with respect to classpath ordering — and the only trace is a debug-level 'Ignored crypto providers' line nobody sees in production, so FIPS-compliance misconfigurations go unnoticed until an audit.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` to no longer throw when multiple `CryptoProvider`s are found; it now sorts by `CryptoProvider::order` descending and returns the first provider, logging the rest only at `debug` (`CryptoIntegration.java`). Since `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, and `FIPS1402Provider` all return `order() = 200` in this diff, a tie means selection falls back to the `ServiceLoader` encounter order (the sort comparator returns 0), which can depend on classpath/service enumeration. This can mask misconfiguration because there is no warning/error when multiple providers are present, and the “Ignored crypto providers” message is debug-only.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Most CryptoProvider methods (getAlgorithmProvider, getPemUtils, getCertificateUtils, getSignature, getAesCbcCipher, getAesGcmCipher, etc.) are unimplemented stubs throwing UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.'), deferring the failure from init to first use. With only the authz-client artifact on the classpath, CryptoIntegration.init() now succeeds (order 100 provider found), so any code path that routes through CryptoIntegration for a non-ECDSA operation — e.g., PEM key parsing or AES-based token decryption shared-code — previously failed at startup with 'Not able to load any cryptoProvider' but now reaches runtime and dies with an UnsupportedOperationException, moving the failure from an early, clear signal to a mid-operation crash far from the configuration cause.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new SPI-registered `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (`META-INF/services/...CryptoProvider`) and calls `CryptoIntegration.init(...)` in `AuthzClient.create(...)`, so initialization can now succeed with only this authz-client provider present. However, `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` leaves most `CryptoProvider` methods as stubs throwing `UnsupportedOperationException` (e.g., `getAlgorithmProvider`, `getPemUtils`, `getCertificateUtils`, `getSignature`, `getAesCbcCipher`, `getAesGcmCipher`, etc.), which can shift failures from provider-detection time to first-use at runtime. The diff alone doesn’t prove those non-ECDSA methods are exercised by authz-client consumers, so it’s an incomplete/integration risk rather than a definitively verifiable functional bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] readSequence() silently returns an empty list for an indefinite-length (0x80) sequence because readLength() returns -1 and the `while (length > 0)` loop never executes, never consuming or validating any content. Corrupt DER input with indefinite-length encoding is reported to the caller as 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2' from asn1derToConcatenatedRS, a misleading error that misdirects debugging toward a sequence-size problem when the actual defect is an unsupported length encoding; readNext() on such an element similarly computes a garbage length (-1 + header bytes consumed) and re-reads from the mark, producing a nonsense element.
matched_golden_ids: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point to the same root problem: indefinite-length encoding makes readLength() return -1, and subsequent length arithmetic/logic treats it as a real length (e.g., subtracting consumed bytes or looping on length > 0), causing incorrect parsing/processing and misleading downstream errors.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()), which on a stock JDK resolves to SUN for PKCS12, not BouncyCastle. Any caller that uses this provider handle to look up or register BC-specific algorithms gets SUN back and fails with NoSuchAlgorithmException (or silently takes a non-BC code path); the name promises BC but the implementation returns whatever provider owns the default keystore type, and a fresh KeyStore instance is constructed per call purely to extract that provider.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is the provider backing the JDK default keystore type (often `SUN`/`SunJSSE` for `PKCS12`), not a BouncyCastle provider. This directly contradicts the `CryptoProvider` interface contract shown in the diff ("Returns bouncycastle provider instance"), so any code expecting an actual BC/BCFIPS `Provider` will receive the wrong provider and may fail when requesting BC-specific algorithms. It also needlessly constructs a new `KeyStore` each call just to read its provider.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] integerToBytes() silently truncates the high-order bytes when qLength < bytes.length, so an r or s value larger than the curve length is chopped instead of rejected. A malformed DER signature whose r/s exceed the component length yields a silently corrupted concatenated signature that fails verification (or signature generation) far downstream with no indication the DER was invalid, sending debuggers hunting through the verification layer instead of pointing at the malformed input; the correct behavior is an IOException, as the seq.size()!=2 check already does for other malformations.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.ECDSACryptoProvider#asn1derToConcatenatedRS, the decoded r/s values are converted via integerToBytes(BigInteger,int). When qLength < bytes.length, integerToBytes truncates the most significant bytes (System.arraycopy(bytes, bytes.length - tmp.length, ...)) without validating that the extra bytes are only a required leading 0x00 for positivity. This means malformed DER integers that are genuinely longer than the expected component size (not just sign-padding) will be silently chopped rather than rejected, producing an incorrect concatenated signature instead of throwing an IOException (unlike other malformations such as seq.size()!=2 which do throw).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The two standalone statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` build encoders whose output is discarded — dead code with no effect on the result. A maintainer reading concatenatedRSToASN1DER can reasonably conclude these encoders contribute to the returned DER (they appear to pre-encode r/s before the real return statement), and any future change to the r/s encoding applied to only one of the three duplicated write sites produces an encoder that passes the round-trip test while diverging in production; both lines pass the deletion test — removing them changes nothing.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` each instantiate a new ASN1Encoder, write to it, and then discard it without using its output. The returned DER is built only by the subsequent `return ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger), ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger)).toByteArray();`. Removing the two standalone statements would not change behavior, but their presence is misleading/maintenance-risk as the finding describes.
